Ange-Félix Patassé (25 January 1937 – 5 April 2011) was a Central African politician who was president of the Central African Republic from 1993 until 2003, when he was deposed by the rebel leader François Bozizé in the 2003 coup d'état. However, during his first term in office (1993–1999), three military mutinies in 1996–1997 led to increasing conflict between so-called "northerners" (like Patassé) and "southerners" (like his predecessor President André Kolingba).

What Ange-Félix Patassé wanted at the start and what Ange-Félix Patassé got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Expatriate mediators and peacekeeping troops were brought in to negotiate peace accords between Patassé and the mutineers and to maintain law and order. During his second term as president, Patassé increasingly lost the support of a number of his long-time allies as well as the French, who had intervened to support him during his first term in office.

The defining trait of Ange-Félix Patassé was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Patassé was ousted in March 2003 and went into exile in Togo. Patassé was born in Paoua, the capital of the northwestern province of Ouham Pendé in the colony of Ubangi-Shari in French Equatorial Africa, and he belonged to the Sara-Kaba ethnic group which predominates in the region around Paoua.

Those who met Ange-Félix Patassé at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Patassé's mother, Véronique Goumba, belonged to the Kare ethnic group of northwestern Ubangi-Shari. As Patassé spent much of his youth in Paoua he was associated with the Ouham-Pendé province and a number of his most loyal political supporters were ethnic Kaba.

The private years of Ange-Félix Patassé explain the public decades better than any speech. After attending school in Ubangi-Shari, Patassé studied in an agricultural institute in Puy-de-Dôme, France, where he received a Technical Baccalaureate which allowed him to enroll in the Superior Academy of Tropical Agriculture in Nogent-sur-Marne, and then in the National Agronomical Institute in Paris. Specializing in zootechnology, he received a diploma from the Center for the Artificial Insemination of Domestic Animals in Rambouillet, France.

The family Ange-Félix Patassé came from matters more than the legends admit. He finished his studies in Paris in 1959, a year before the independence of the Central African Republic. Patassé joined the Central African civil service in 1959, shortly before independence.

The first real success of Ange-Félix Patassé arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. He became an agricultural engineer and agricultural inspector in the Ministry of Agriculture in July 1963, under President David Dacko. In December 1965, Dacko appointed him Director of Agriculture and Minister of Development.

The last chapter of Ange-Félix Patassé was written long after the fame. Patassé was the "cousin" of President Bokassa's principal wife, Catherine Denguiadé, and gained the confidence of the new president, serving in almost all the governments formed by Bokassa. During this period Patassé followed Bokassa in becoming a convert to Islam for a few months, and changed his name to Mustafa Patassé.

The whole life of Ange-Félix Patassé reads like a single decision repeated. After Bokassa became Emperor Bokassa I, Patassé was named Prime Minister and Head of the first Imperial Government. He remained in this position for 2 1/2 years, when a public announcement was made that Patassé had stepped down from office due to health problems.

Between the birth and the legend of Ange-Félix Patassé lie the years that actually decide it. Patassé then left for France, where he remained in exile until the overthrow of Bokassa in September 1979. Shortly before Bokassa's overthrow, Patassé announced his opposition to the Emperor and founded the Front de Libération du Peuple Centrafricain (FLPC; Front for the Liberation of the Central African People).

The reputation of Ange-Félix Patassé was built in the middle, not at the edges. Emperor Bokassa was overthrown and President David Dacko restored to power by the French in 1979. Patassé attempted to escape to Chad, but failed and was arrested again.

Somebody like Ange-Félix Patassé should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. The Patassé government was the first government of the Central African Empire, created immediately after Bokassa crowned himself Emperor. His government was tasked with managing the transition from republic to empire, implementing imperial reforms, and preparing for the extravagant coronation of 1977.

The life of Ange-Félix Patassé begins far from where the story usually starts. Growing internal tensions and Bokassa’s suspicions led to Patassé’s dismissal in July 1978, after which Henri Maïdou replaced him as Prime Minister. Patassé returned to the CAR to present himself as a candidate for the presidential election of 15 March 1981, after which it was announced that Patassé gained 38% of the votes and thus came in second, after President Dacko.

Ange-Félix Patassé was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Several months later, on 1 September 1981, General André Kolingba overthrew Dacko in a bloodless coup and took power, after which he forbade political activity in the country. Four days later, having failed to gain the support of the military forces, Patassé went in disguise to the French Embassy to seek refuge.

To understand where Ange-Félix Patassé ended up, start with where Ange-Félix Patassé began. After heated negotiations between President Kolingba and the French, Patassé was allowed to leave for exile in Togo. After remaining abroad for almost a decade, of which several years were spent in France, Patassé returned to the Central African Republic in 1992 to participate in presidential elections as head of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People (MLPC).

The road from the beginning to the peak of Ange-Félix Patassé ran through years nobody filmed. The donor community, with the fall of the Soviet Union, saw no need to prop up the Kolingba regime and so had pressed for change helping to organize elections with some help from the UN Electoral Assistance Unit and with logistical support from the French army. After the Kolingba regime sabotaged a first set of elections in 1992, a second set of elections was held.

Each stage of the life of Ange-Félix Patassé made the next stage possible. On the second round on 19 September 1993, Patassé came in first with 37 percent of the vote, well ahead of his nearest competitors, Kolingba, David Dacko and Abel Goumba. Largely thanks to the foreign pressure notably from the US and technical support from the UN, for the first time the elections were fair and democratic.

The people who knew Ange-Félix Patassé young describe someone already restless. Patassé thus became the first president in the nation's history to gain power by such means. When he took office on 22 October 1993; it marked the first (and to date, only) time in the country's history that a sitting government peacefully surrendered power to the opposition.

What Ange-Félix Patassé built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. During Patassé's first six-year term in office (22 October 1993 – 1999), the economy appeared to improve a little as the flow of donor money started up again following the elections and the apparent legitimacy they brought. Patassé had the support of most of his own Sara-Kaba people, the largest ethno-linguistic group in the Central African Republic, as well as the Souma people of his "hometown" of Paoua and the Kare people of his mother.

By the time Ange-Félix Patassé reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. As a populist, Patassé promoted himself as a candidate who represented a majority of the population against the privileges of southerners who held a disproportionate number of lucrative jobs in the public and parastatal sectors of the economy. Most notably, the Yakoma people had already obtained access to European education in the colonial era and were systematically favored under the presidency of Kolingba.

The rise of Ange-Félix Patassé was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. As President, Patassé lowered the pay of the Yakoma-dominated army corps (which he distrusted), and conversely created a well-paid presidential guard and other militias mainly composed of "northerners". This reversal of a long-standing ethnic inequality heightened tensions in the country and quickly pitted officers and soldiers against Patassé.

Setbacks came early for Ange-Félix Patassé, and the response to them is the real story. Destruction of buildings and property during these rebellions had an adverse impact on the economy. Patassé's government successfully regained control with the help of François Bozizé and the French, but his obvious dependency on the French, against whom he had regularly railed, reduced his standing further.

The legacy of Ange-Félix Patassé outlived the circumstances that produced it. His subsequent use of Libyan troops as a body guard did nothing to help his reputation, either locally or with the donor community and the US even closed their embassy temporarily. The last and most serious mutiny continued until early 1997, when a semblance of order was restored after the signing of the Bangui Agreements, and with the help of troops from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal, and Togo.

Few lives travel as far as that of Ange-Félix Patassé, and the distance is the point. The Security Council of the United Nations approved a mission for peace, MINURCA, in 1998. These mutinies greatly increased the tension between "northerners" and "southerners" in the CAR and thus polarized society to a greater extent than before.

The childhood of Ange-Félix Patassé contains the adult in small print. In the presidential election of September 1999, Patassé won easily, defeating former presidents Kolingba and Dacko. In May 2001, a failed coup attempt against Patassé took place, in which Kolingba and possibly Bozizé were involved.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Ange-Félix Patassé — in that order. Both of these officers left the country to evade trial: Kolingba for Uganda, Bozizé for Chad along with military forces that were loyal to him. In the aftermath of the 2001 coup attempt, the Yakoma were targeted by the Patassé government in reprisal attacks.

The turning point in the life of Ange-Félix Patassé looked like a failure at the time. Several of these killings took place in broad daylight on the streets of Bangui. Over the course of the following two years, foreign fighters from Libya as well as Congolese rebels from the MLC (led by Jean-Pierre Bemba) were deployed in combat against Bozizé loyalists.

Every biography of Ange-Félix Patassé has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. The MLC was later found guilty by the International Criminal Court (ICC) of committing war crimes during this intervention, including murder, rape, pillaging and torture. In October 2002, another coup attempt took place, this time carried out by Bozizé who had returned from Chad with his militias.

The education of Ange-Félix Patassé happened mostly outside any school. After a week of fighting, the Patassé government, aided by the Libyans and MLC fighters, emerged victorious. The government was again criticized for widespread human rights abuses by its troops including sexual violence and the killing of dozens to a hundred Chadian nationals in Bangui; additionally, Patassé cracked down on the press.

What Ange-Félix Patassé wanted at the start and what Ange-Félix Patassé got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Patassé left the country for a conference in Niger in 2003, and in his absence Bozizé seized Bangui on March 15. Although this takeover was internationally condemned, no attempt was made to depose the new leader.

The defining trait of Ange-Félix Patassé was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Although nominated as the MLPC's presidential candidate in November 2004, on 30 December 2004 Patassé was barred from running in the 2005 presidential election due to what the Constitutional Court considered problems with his birth certificate and land title. After an agreement signed in Libreville, Gabon on 22 January 2005, all barred presidential candidates were permitted to stand in the March 13 election except for Patassé, on the grounds that he was the subject of judicial proceedings.

Those who met Ange-Félix Patassé at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. The MLPC instead backed his last prime minister, Martin Ziguélé, for president. Patassé was accused of stealing 70 billion Central African francs from the country's treasury.

The private years of Ange-Félix Patassé explain the public decades better than any speech. He denied this and in an interview with Agence France-Presse on 21 December 2004, he stated that he had no idea where he could have found so much money to steal in a country with a budget of only 90–100 billion francs. He was also accused of war crimes in connection with the violence that followed a failed 2002 coup attempt, in which rebels from the northern Democratic Republic of the Congo came to Patassé's assistance, but were accused of committing multiple atrocities in the process.
